title: Hammir Singh Wins Back Chittor
subtitle: The Mountain Throne Rises Again
era: Sisodia restoration, c. 1326-1337 CE; reign c. 1326-1364 CE
region: Chittor and the hill country of Mewar
moral: Recovery is built by patience as much as bravery.

sources.citation: Nayachandra Suri, Hammir Mahakavya, c. 1400 CE
sources.note: Earliest extended literary account of Hammir; a Sanskrit kavya to read critically.

sources.citation: Kumbhalgarh Prashasti, 1460 CE; Jain temple inscription of 1438 CE
sources.note: Retrospective but important epigraphic evidence for Hammir and a victory over a Sultanate force.

sources.citation: Dasharatha Sharma, Rajasthan Through the Ages (1966); R.V. Somani, History of Mewar (1976)
sources.note: Standard reconstructions of Hammir's restoration and the Singoli tradition.

dialogue.text: After Alauddin Khalji broke Chittor, the hills of Mewar fell silent. A generation later, one Sisodia prince dared to climb back and restore the lost mountain throne: Hammir Singh.
In 1303, Alauddin Khalji’s armies stormed Chittor. The old Guhila line was broken, the fort garrison replaced, and for years the high rock watched the plains under new masters.

panels.shot: slow push-in from wide landscape to scattered hill hamlet

dialogue.text: Yet the hills of Mewar were not empty. Rajput clans, scattered and bruised, clung to ravines and outcrops, nursing memories of Chittor and waiting for a leader.

panels.shot: intimate medium shot around a village fire

dialogue.text: From these years of loss emerges Hammir Singh. The later Hammir Mahakavya will wrap his youth in poetry, but all agree: he grew up in the shadow of a fallen fort and a wounded name.
By the 1320s, while Delhi changed from Khalji to Tughlaq, Hammir gathered men, revenues and alliances in the hill country. Each small fort taken, each levy raised, stitched Mewar back together.
Delhi’s gaze lay on Deccan campaigns and rebellions. Hammir watched the gaps. The inscriptions speak not of a sudden miracle, but of patient expansion from village to outpost, from outpost to fort.

dialogue.speaker: maharana_hammir_singh
dialogue.text: We win Mewar not by rage alone, but by joining every hill and hand.
By mid-century, Hammir stands clear in the sources: a Sisodia lord holding key hill-forts, levying taxes, protecting caravans. The memory of Guhila rule begins to take a new name: Mewar of Hammir.
But Delhi still claimed Chittor. Under Muhammad bin Tughlaq, governors and garrisons held its heights. To reach the old capital, Hammir first had to meet the Sultanate in the field.
Tradition remembers Singoli as the turning field. Inscriptions from later years speak proudly of a victory over the Sultan. Exact maneuvers are lost, but the outcome is clear: Hammir’s banner held.

Later tales will say he captured Muhammad bin Tughlaq himself. Persian chronicles, close to the court, are silent. What survives beyond doubt is this: a Tughlaq force was beaten, and Mewar’s confidence surged.

panels.shot: post-battle wide with emphasis on aftermath, not combat

dialogue.speaker: maharana_hammir_singh
dialogue.text: Remember this ground. We win a throne, but we also inherit its burdens.

panels.shot: long shot of marching column toward distant fort

dialogue.text: With the Sultanate pushed back in the region, the path to Chittor lay open. Between about 1326 and 1337, in a slow press of campaigns, Hammir moved from hill forts to the mountain citadel itself.

The records do not detail every assault and parley. They speak instead of the result: Chittor, once a Khalji prize, returned to Rajput hands under Hammir, and the Sisodia standard climbed the ramparts.

panels.shot: triumphant but restrained high-angle inside the fort

dialogue.text: The Kumbhalgarh prasasti, written later in the fifteenth century, looks back and names him restorer. It remembers not only battle, but the reopening of shrines, the return of merchants, the hum of life within the walls.

panels.shot: medium shot at a temple plinth

dialogue.text: A Jain inscription of 1438, recalling these times, links Hammir’s name to protection and victory. Patrons once again dared to endow temples and markets, expecting their gifts to outlast a single ruler’s life.

Hammir reigned into the 1360s. The details of his court remain sparse, but the pattern is clear: tribute balanced with defiance, hill alliances tended, and the Sisodia house rooted firmly in Mewar’s soil.

panels.shot: montage-like wide, ghosted future figures behind

dialogue.text: Later centuries would pile legend on his name, casting Hammir as the first great restorer in a line that faced new sultans and new empires. Through him, Mewar’s Rajput identity found a story of loss and return.

Hammir Singh’s climb back to Chittor shows how thrones are truly won—not by one blaze of glory, but by years of patient rebuilding—until a broken mountain once again has a guardian, and a people remember their name.
